visible.summary:
Zamfara is where Nigeria's Sharia criminal-law wave began: its governor introduced the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, and by 2002 eleven more northern states followed — a parallel system of Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, which the 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms is still operative and capital-punishment-capable for same-sex acts. A 2019 rights-monitoring study of 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 uses Zamfara as one of three sample states, confirming the courts function in practice, not just on paper.

No capital sentence is on record as imposed in Zamfara, and no trans-specific incident appears in the dossier; the finding is pioneering the bloc's enforcement architecture and hosting functioning religious courts.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalisation is the adjacent layer here: the federal SSMPA (up to 14 years, applies to tourists) plus the Sharia penal layer for Muslims shape police and Hisbah posture toward any gender-nonconforming presence, even though the written offences target conduct rather than gender identity.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch report (2004) on the extension of Sharia to criminal law in Nigeria: Zamfara's governor was first, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999 (in force 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation - to date the only states where Sharia courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

Primary state-authored account of Zamfara's Sharia adoption, written by Alh. Ahmed Bello Mahmud, then Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Zamfara State, and presented at a JNI-sponsored seminar on 6 July 2000. It details Zamfara's enabling legislation - the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999 under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution - which established Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction in Islamic law and enabled the codification of a Sharia Penal Code, and records the Grand Kadi taking over court administration from 29 June 2000 alongside policy moves against prostitution and gambling. For this record it documents from inside the state government the adoption process that began Nigeria's Sharia criminal-law wave in Zamfara.

Academic reconstruction of how Zamfara's Sharia Penal Code was made: the Zamfara governor appointed a committee in June 1999 mandated to study implementing Sharia including the full scope of Islamic criminal law, and by the end of 2000 eleven other northern states had adopted the application of Sharia. The chapter analyses the codification of offences and punishments and the penal-code architecture the Sharia courts of the twelve states apply, grounding this record's claim that Zamfara pioneered the bloc's religious-criminal framework.

visible.summary:
Borno is one of the twelve northern Nigerian states applying Sharia criminal law in parallel with the federal system since the 1999–2002 wave. A June 2025 government country-of-origin note lists Borno among the states where the Sharia penal code remains in force for Muslims, criminalising same-sex acts between men (death penalty the maximum) and between women (penalties up to flogging and imprisonment), with a dedicated section on enforcement and the religious police — the legal architecture, not a case record, is the finding.

No trans-specific incident, no Hisbah case and no court-level study covers Borno in this dossier; the bloc's own reporting caveat is that enforcement data capture only a fraction of actual cases, so silence is not evidence of safety. The federal criminal code's coverage of men's acts (up to 14 years) applies here as everywhere in Nigeria.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalisation is the adjacent layer here: the federal SSMPA (up to 14 years, applies to tourists) plus the Sharia penal layer for Muslims shape police and Hisbah posture toward any gender-nonconforming presence, even though the written offences target conduct rather than gender identity.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Insurgency-related violence and military operations in the northeast affect all travellers in this state; only trans-specific risk is assessed.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Borno among the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law.

UK Home Office country-of-origin information note (June 2025) on sexual orientation and gender identity in Nigeria: Islamic law applies to Muslims in the 12 northern states and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' for men is death in all 12 states and penalties for 'lesbianism' range from death to flogging and imprisonment; includes a dedicated section on enforcement of Sharia provisions and the attitude of the hisbah (morality police).

Ostien's Volume III reproduces Borno State's own statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities (2000), gazetted in Borno State Gazette No. 42 Vol. 26 on 18 October 2001 and signed by Governor Kachalla on 10 December 2000. Section 3 makes engaging in prostitution, lesbianism, a homosexual act or pimping an offence in the State; Section 7 provides that any person who 'engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender shall upon conviction be punished with death'; Section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement; and Section 9 assigns jurisdiction to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts. Borno's own enacted death penalty for same-gender intercourse independently supports this record's finding that the state's legal architecture, not just the national framework, criminalises same-sex conduct.

The sourcebook's list of enacted Sharia Penal Codes records Borno's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 3 March 2003, with no operation date or gazette identified; the editor notes the Borno text was obtained only in May 2006, after the volume's annotation had been completed, which is why Borno is not among the individually annotated codes. Confirms Borno enacted its own state Sharia Penal Code legislation in addition to its secular morality law, so the record's claimed parallel Sharia layer for Borno rests on a Borno-specific enactment rather than mere umbrella coverage.

visible.summary:
Gombe applies Sharia criminal law as part of the twelve-state northern bloc adopted by 2002. The Sharia layer criminalises conduct beyond the federal SSMPA, including same-sex acts between women; the framework applies to Muslims, and its practical reach over visitors is mediated by arrest practice - including hisbah morality policing in the northern block - rather than by any formal 'tourists excepted' rule. No trans-specific incident or documented Hisbah activity appears in this dossier for Gombe. Reporting-decay caveats apply: absence of records reflects fear of outing and surveillance gaps, not absence of risk.

Score 0.024 below the national 0.08. Tied with the generic-Sharia tier (Borno, Jigawa, Kaduna, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger): the enacted parallel criminal system is the deviation, without additional case-level or enforcement evidence to push further. Well above Kano (0.03) and Bauchi (0.02), which have death-penalty text or carried-out capital sentences respectively.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalisation is the adjacent layer here: the federal SSMPA (up to 14 years, applies to tourists) plus the Sharia penal layer for Muslims shape police and Hisbah posture toward any gender-nonconforming presence, even though the written offences target conduct rather than gender identity.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Gombe among the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law.

UK Home Office country-of-origin information note (June 2025) on sexual orientation and gender identity in Nigeria: Islamic law applies to Muslims in the 12 northern states and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' for men is death in all 12 states and penalties for 'lesbianism' range from death to flogging and imprisonment; includes a dedicated section on enforcement of Sharia provisions and the attitude of the hisbah (morality police).

In October 2023 the Gombe State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) raided a homosexual birthday gathering at Duwa Plaza along the Bauchi-Gombe Expressway that was preparing a same-sex wedding, arresting 76 people; state PRO Buhari Sa'ad told reporters that 59 males were detained with 21 wilfully confessing to being homosexuals, along with 17 females present at the scene, and that they 'will be charged to court to answer for their crime which is on social vice; a crime in Gombe State.' The first incident-level evidence in this dossier that Gombe enforces its moral-crimes layer on the ground, with local charging of attendees.

The Lagos daily The Guardian, byline James Agberebi, published 23 October 2023, reports that about 76 people were arrested after a tip-off about a same-sex birthday party and planned marriage in Gombe State; Gombe NSCDC Commandant Mohammed Muazu confirmed the arrests, spokesperson Buhari Saad said 21 of the 59 detained males were involved in gay activities while the remaining males and the 17 females were invited guests and onlookers, and officers voiced concern over the participants' ages. Independent Lagos-press confirmation of the same October 2023 Gombe mass arrest, archived from the live Guardian Nigeria URL on 4 December 2023.

The annotated volume records Gombe's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 23 November 2001, and annotates its text: Gombe, Jigawa, Kano and Zamfara share the sodomy offence punishing unmarried men with caning of 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment and married men with stoning to death (rajm); the lesbianism offence carries up to 50 lashes plus imprisonment of up to six months; and Gombe defines gross indecency in its own formulation as 'any sexual offence against the normal or usual standards of behaviour.' The state's enacted statutory text behind this record's claim that Gombe's Sharia layer criminalises same-sex conduct by men and women beyond the federal code.

visible.summary:
Jigawa is among the twelve northern Nigerian states whose Sharia penal codes, adopted in the 1999–2002 wave, give religious courts criminal jurisdiction over Muslims. A June 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms Jigawa's code remains in force, criminalising same-sex sexual acts by men (death the maximum) and by women (flogging and up to six months' imprisonment) — coverage the federal code, which reaches only men's acts, does not supply independently.

No trans-specific incident, Hisbah record or court-level study covers Jigawa in this dossier; like the rest of the bloc its enforcement statistics are acknowledged as partial. The finding is the enacted parallel jurisdiction and its statutory reach over women's conduct.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalisation is the adjacent layer here: the federal SSMPA (up to 14 years, applies to tourists) plus the Sharia penal layer for Muslims shape police and Hisbah posture toward any gender-nonconforming presence, even though the written offences target conduct rather than gender identity.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch report (2004) on the extension of Sharia to criminal law in Nigeria: Zamfara's governor was first, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999 (in force 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation - to date the only states where Sharia courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

The UK Home Office's June 2025 country note carries a twelve-state Sharia penalties table with Jigawa's own row: Sharia Penal Code (2000) — 'Married men: death by stoning,' 'Unmarried men: 100 lashes and imprisonment for up to one year,' and up to 50 lashes with imprisonment for up to 6 months for same-sex acts between women; section 8.2.20 points to the note's Sharia section on the codes in force in Kano, Borno, Kaduna and other northern states. Dated government confirmation that Jigawa's Sharia penal layer remains the operative criminal frame for Muslims in the state, matching this record's June 2025 country-of-origin note claim.

The sourcebook lists Jigawa's Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, Law No. 12 of 2000, signed into law on 18 December 2000 and coming into operation on 27 December 2000 (Jigawa State Gazette Vol. 1 No. 12), and annotates Jigawa among the four states (with Gombe, Kano and Zamfara) whose sodomy offence punishes unmarried men with 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment and married men with stoning to death (rajm); lesbianism carries up to 50 lashes plus up to six months' imprisonment, with Jigawa including the 'unnatural fusion of the female sexual organs' explanation of the offence. Enactment-level detail for the record's claim that Jigawa's 1999-2002-wave code criminalises acts the federal code does not reach, including women's same-sex conduct.

visible.summary:
Kaduna carries both layers of criminalisation that define Nigeria's northern bloc. Its 2017 secular Penal Code punishes 'unnatural offences' — covering acts between men and between women — with up to 21 years' imprisonment plus fine; and, per a June 2025 government country-of-origin note, the state's Sharia penal code additionally applies to Muslims through religious courts with criminal jurisdiction, in force since the 1999–2002 wave, with the bloc's capital maximum for men's acts.

No trans-specific incident or documented Hisbah enforcement appears for Kaduna in this dossier, and no court-level study samples it. The finding is the stacked architecture: a long-term secular offence alongside a parallel religious jurisdiction, both current.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalisation is the adjacent layer here: the federal SSMPA (up to 14 years, applies to tourists) plus the Sharia penal layer for Muslims shape police and Hisbah posture toward any gender-nonconforming presence, even though the written offences target conduct rather than gender identity.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch report (2004) on the extension of Sharia to criminal law in Nigeria: Zamfara's governor was first, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999 (in force 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation - to date the only states where Sharia courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

The UK Home Office's June 2025 country note carries Kaduna's own row in its twelve-state Sharia penalties table (section 8.4.3, ILGA-derived): Kaduna's Sharia Penal Code Law (2002) with death by stoning as the maximum for liwat (sodomy) and same-sex acts between women punishable 'at the discretion of the qadi (Sharia court judge)'. Section 3.1.6 and 8.2.19 add that Kaduna separately adopted its own secular Penal Code in 2017, whose Section 259 punishes 'unnatural offences' - sodomy, lesbianism, bestiality - with up to 21 years' imprisonment and a fine, above the federal 14-year ceiling. Dated government confirmation of the two-layer criminalisation this record claims: a harsher Kaduna-specific secular statute plus a parallel Sharia layer applying to Muslims.

Ostien's annotated volume lists Kaduna's Sharia Penal Code Law 2002, Law No. 4 of 2002, signed into law and coming into operation on 21 June 2002 (Kaduna State Gazette No. 17 Vol. 36, 4 July 2002, pp. A15-A108, bound with the Sharia Criminal Procedure Code), and its annotation records that Kaduna is one of only three states whose enacted text states 'Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)' - with no unmarried/married graduation - while the lesbianism offence is left to ta'azir (discretionary punishment). Enactment-level evidence that Kaduna's Sharia layer is its own promulgated parallel criminal code carrying the bloc's capital ceiling for men's same-sex acts, confirming this record's stacked-architecture finding without relying on umbrella coverage.

visible.summary:
In May 2018 in Ekpoma, a community discovered two men having sex; one was lynched to death and the other escaped. The coverage framed the act as an 'abominable' one defying 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land', and no prosecution is recorded: customary moral judgement operating lethally, with complete impunity. For national context, a rights-monitoring report published in January 2025 documented 556 violations against real or perceived LGBT people affecting 850 victims across Nigeria in 2024 — and states these are only a fraction of the true scale.

Edo's finding is the Ekpoma killing itself: where a discovered visitor can face lethal 'community justice' invoked in the name of tradition, answered afterwards by nobody.
visible.tangentialFactors: The documented lethal incidents here concern male same-sex conduct rather than gender expression directly; their weight for trans visitors is the demonstrated capacity for community-justice killing with impunity in a customary-authority setting.

sources.claim: Nigerian Observer (May 2018): in Ekpoma a mob lynched one of two men caught together and the other escaped, framed as an 'abominable act' under traditional heritage. Documents fatal community violence in Edo State.

The Initiative for Equal Rights (TIERs) '2024 Human Rights Violations Report' (published January 2025): annual documentation of violations based on real or perceived SOGIESC in Nigeria; per the dossier, its 2024 edition records 556 violations affecting 850 victims across the reporting period and states these represent only a fraction of the true scale.

On 10 June 2010 The Nigerian Observer reported from Benin City (Oredo LGA, Edo State) that a middle-aged man, Mark Osato Edomwonyi, narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was caught in a same-sex act with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment; a neighbour raised the alarm and Mark fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, which then 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution is recorded in the report, and Mark's whereabouts were still unknown at filing. First incident-level evidence for Edo beyond the 2018 Ekpoma killing: lethal mob 'community justice' operates in the state capital too, with no documented law-enforcement response.

The Nigerian Observer reported on 15 August 2008 that police declared Ugbogbo Ovbukhan wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner Jerry were caught in the act in a remote community in Edo State in February 2008; a mob mercilessly beat the two for desecrating the community, Ovbukhan escaped before police arrived, and the police arrested Jerry for interrogation. Direct evidence that Edo's police machinery pursued same-sex couples on the ground in 2008 — a community lynching attempt answered by arrest and a wanted declaration rather than protection.
